subLevels.german: Es gibt vier Jahreszeiten: Frühling, Sommer, Herbst und Winter.
subLevels.reveal: Zeit = "time" (as in "zeitgeist"), so Jahreszeit = "time of year". Herbst ~ "harvest", as you may have guessed. Frühling has no cognate in English but it roughly means "the early one".

subLevels.german: Im Frühling gibt es viele Blumen.

hints.hint: We've seen viel(e) before in Ich habe zu viel Wein getrunken. 🥂🥴
The singular is Blume. Does it sound like an English word you know?

subLevels.reveal: Out of the words for 🌸 the oldest English word is "blossom". English then got "bloom" as a borrowing from Old Norse in the Viking invasions of Britain. So English has two cognates of Blume at its disposal. Another conquest - the Normans - brought "flower" from French "fleur" into the language.

subLevels.instruction: Match the weather words (−1 pt per wrong placement)
subLevels.reveal: -ig ~ "-y" and -isch is just "-ish", so Germans literally say it's "rain-ish"!

hints.hint: Think a common form of precipitation seen im Winter.

subLevels.reveal: Es in Es gibt "there is/are" and in Es schneit are the same "it". It doesn't refer to anything specific, it's just a grammatical placeholder that needs to be filled to keep the grammar happy. Whereas English goes with "there" for existence and "it" elsewhere, German very economically uses "es" whenever it needs a dummy subject.

hints.hint: Schnee is the noun form of the verb we just saw.

subLevels.reveal: gleich and "(a)like" are direct cognates! They descended from Proto-Germanic *ga-līkaz. English usually dropped the prefix, but sometimes retained it as a fossilised "a-" as in "alike" ("among" is another example!). Meanwhile, German fused the prefix and stem together so the prefix is no longer visible.

subLevels.german: Im Winter trägt man warme Kleidung.
subLevels.reveal: Kleidung has not one but two cognates in English — "clothing" and "cladding" (clothing for buildings!). We also retain the verb form "clad" as in "clad in shining armour", but it sounds a little medieval.

subLevels.german: Magst du sonniges Wetter oder kaltes Wetter?

hints.hint: We saw a different version of this verb before in Ich möchte nicht arbeiten!.

subLevels.reveal: Personally I'm for sonniges UND kaltes Wetter.

subLevels.german: Ein Regenmantel ist eine Art Kleidung.

hints.hint: Regenmantel = Regen + Mantel. You know Regen. Mantel ~ "mantle" — a large covering garment.
Art ~ "sort/kind" — as in the archaic English "after this art" meaning "of this kind".

subLevels.reveal: Mantel ~ "mantle" — as in the mantle of leadership, or the earth's mantle — all from the same root of a large covering garment. And Kleid ~ "clad" ~ "cloak" — there's a whole cluster of covering and clothing words that go back to the same idea of wrapping yourself up against the elements.

subLevels.german: Es regnet und regnet und regnet. Das Wetter ist so schlecht!

hints.hint: regnet is the verb form of Regen — rain.
schlecht is the opposite of gut — as in Guten Tag!

subLevels.reveal: This sentence is likely to be applicable between 1/3 and 1/2 of the time in Germany. But of course Germans won't take that lying down...

subLevels.german: Es gibt kein schlechtes Wetter, nur schlechte Kleidung.

hints.hint: kein ~ "no/none" — we saw it in the Karfreitag sentence.
nur ~ "only" — it narrows things down to one option.

subLevels.reveal: This is probably not German in origin, but it's a sentiment that Germans have definitely embraced. It might be paired with the admonition Du bist doch nicht aus Zucker! "C'mon, you're not made of...?"
